config.prompt: Resting ventilation is about 0.5 L per breath × 12 breaths/min ≈ 6 L/min. Elite endurance athletes at maximal effort exceed roughly what ventilation?
config.why: 150–200 L/min and more — enormous headroom, which is why in most healthy people the lungs are not the limiting factor in maximal performance.
config.context: Arterial blood leaves the lungs about 95–98% saturated with oxygen even at maximal effort.

activities.anchor: breathlessness means your lungs are maxed out
activities.caption: true or false — the breathless runner
activities.name: hlBreathJudge

statements.s: Ventilation can be pushed far past what the circulation can use.
statements.why: The respiratory system has enormous headroom — the bottleneck sits further along the chain.

statements.s: Breathlessness in hard exercise means the lungs are maxed out.
statements.why: Breathlessness is driven largely by rising CO₂ — a chemical signal, not a full tank.

statements.s: Arterial blood leaves the lungs about 95–98% saturated even at maximal effort.
statements.why: Only elite athletes in extreme cases show small desaturation — their pumps outrunning their lungs.

statements.s: Sustaining ventilation near 150 L/min is free — breathing costs no blood flow.
statements.why: Heavily working breathing muscles steal blood flow from the limbs — the body pays for breathing from the same cardiac output.

activities.caption: rest vs maximal exercise — file the circulation's numbers
activities.name: hlCircSort

config.prompt: One circulation, two states — file each claim:

items.label: working muscle receives about 15–20% of cardiac output
stroke volume near 200 mL in the elite endurance athlete
working muscle receives 80–85% of cardiac output
gut and kidneys accept less as regulated shunting ramps up
haemoglobin holds about a litre of oxygen in transit

config.why: The elite's 35–40 L/min against the untrained 20–22 is the single largest physiological gap between the fit and the elite — built by a bigger left ventricle and expanded blood volume.

activities.caption: place the elite ceiling on the scale
activities.name: hlVomaxPlace

config.prompt: Place the VO₂max (ml/kg/min) where elite male distance runners and cross-country skiers sit:
config.why: 70–90+, against 35–45 in untrained young adults and 50–60 in regular recreational runners — the highest credibly measured values near 96–97.

activities.anchor: no longer balance production with clearance
activities.caption: the training stack that raises the sustainable fraction
activities.name: hlStackOrder

config.prompt: The threshold-raising stack, laid out in order:
items: Easy-volume work builds the aerobic base and mitochondria
Tempo runs at threshold intensity teach the system to clear lactate at higher rates
Interval work pushes the ceiling itself
Re-test the field marker every six to eight weeks
config.why: The untrained reach threshold around 55–65% of VO₂max; trained distance athletes sustain 80–90% — and elite marathoners race 42.2 km close to it.

activities.caption: one session vs the training age — drag the divider
activities.name: hlAcuteCompare

config.prompt: The same body, two timescales — drag the divider:

before.label: the acute response — one session
before.text: heart rate rises before the muscles even start; stroke volume maxes around 40–50% of VO₂max; systolic pressure spikes; plasma volume shrinks toward sweat

after.label: the chronic adaptation — weeks to months
after.text: plasma volume up first, then mitochondria and capillaries; stroke volume and cardiac output up; resting heart rate down — 40–50 bpm in serious endurance athletes is unremarkable

config.why: Resting measures are the honest cheap tests: a rising resting heart rate across days signals fatigue, illness or under-fuelling.

activities.caption: one line of this zone-setting is wrong — click it
activities.name: hlZoneSpot

config.prompt: One line of this zone-setting routine is wrong — click it:
lines: Estimate maximum heart rate with 220 − age — it predicts the population average, not you.
The formula's individual error is about ±2 bpm, so treat its zones as a ruler.
Better: field-test your own maximum, or anchor zones to threshold pace or power.
Use heart rate as a drift gauge — cardiac drift tells you about the day, not the zones.
A polarised week runs roughly 80% easy, 20% hard.
config.correction: The individual error is about ±10–12 bpm — a 10-bpm miss shifts every zone, which is why zones get field-tested or anchored to threshold.
config.why: The five-zone model organises intensity fine; the arithmetic underneath is a population average wearing a personal disguise.

activities.anchor: the anti-doping line is a rule
activities.caption: the altitude protocol — pair each piece with its dose
activities.name: hlAltMatch

config.prompt: Live high, train low — match each piece of the protocol:

pairs.right: roughly 2,000–2,500 m — enough hypoxia to trigger erythropoiesis
below about 1,250 m, so interval quality survives
about four weeks, per Levine and Stray-Gundersen's controlled 1997 study
roughly 1–3% at sea level — small, but decisive in championship fields

config.why: Responders vary substantially, and the dose must be managed — excessive erythropoiesis thickens blood and raises clot risk, one reason haemoglobin levels are capped in competition.
